In particular, the proposal to impose a one-time 30-year service period or a 55-year age limit for serving employees has necessitated a serious debate on the stability of the civil service, employees' rights to service security, and the future of the merit system.

The institutional basis of Nepal's modern civil service is considered to be the Civil Service Act published on 22 Bhadra, 2013. Before that, there were administrative personnel structures during the Malla, Shah, and Rana periods. After the Act and Regulations of 2013, a new Civil Service Act was issued in 2049 and the Regulations in 2050. The Act and Regulations were amended in 2064 in accordance with political changes.

The 2072 Constitution provided for the formation and operation of government services at the federal, provincial, and local levels according to the federal system of governance. However, a federal civil service law could not be formulated accordingly. The bill was repeatedly withdrawn or inactivated after reaching parliament. As a result, many problems arose in the federal structure in terms of employee management, adjustment, career development, and service conditions.

Meanwhile, the civil service has played a continuous role in the running of the state, facing challenges from the political changes of 2017, 2046, and 2063 to the referendum of 2036, earthquakes, floods, and landslides, and the COVID-19 pandemic. Despite changes in political leadership and government, the civil service has functioned as a permanent mechanism to implement state policies and decisions.

However, the lack of a federal civil service law has led to inequality and confusion in employee management. The terms of service of permanent, adjusted, contract and salaried employees at the federal, provincial and local levels are different. Some receive pensions from the federal government, some receive gratuities from the former local bodies, while the post-retirement benefits of some are uncertain. Although all seven provinces have enacted civil service laws, the lack of a federal basic law has not resulted in uniformity in the overall system.

In such a situation, it is both the government's need and responsibility to enact a federal civil service law. But weakening the service conditions and security of employees in the name of enacting laws is not the solution.

The proposal to impose a one-time 30-year service period or 55-year age limit for employees in the Federal Civil Service Bill has created controversy. Supporters of the proposal have argued that the upper echelons of the administration have long been dominated by employees of the same generation, delaying decision-making processes and obstructing the path to promotion. They say that such a provision is necessary to provide opportunities to the new generation and ensure generational transition in the administrative structure.

But there are serious arguments against it. When a large number of experienced employees leave at once, there may be a vacuum at the policy and decision-making levels of the administration. Institutional knowledge and experience may be lost. Administrative delays, poor service delivery, and decision-making problems are not only created by the age or length of service of the employees. Behind them are also political interference, weak management, systemic problems, and lack of accountability.

Another important question is the trust between the employee and the state regarding the terms of service. When an employee enters the service, he or she has made a career plan based on the prevailing laws. After dedicating the energetic time of his or her life to service, if the rules are changed in the middle and sent to retirement, it affects both personal life and trust in the state.

An employee who enters service at the age of 23 will be 54 after serving for 31 years. He may have planned his life with the expectation of remaining in service for 58 or 60 years. If such an employee is suddenly removed from service, the pension he will receive based on 30 years of service alone will not be able to compensate for the financial and professional losses he will suffer for the rest of his life. As he grows older, his ability to work may decrease, but experience, maturity and institutional knowledge also increase with it. Therefore, it is not appropriate to make age the only criterion for efficiency.

Article 285 of the Constitution of Nepal provides for the formation and operation of government services at the federal, provincial and local levels. There is also a constitutional provision that the principles of openness and inclusiveness should be adopted when filling positions in government services.

Section 58 of the current Civil Service Act, 2049 BS, protects the terms and conditions of service of employees. This section provides that the terms and conditions of salary, gratuity, pension and other benefits applicable at the time of appointment of an employee cannot be changed in a manner that adversely affects them without their consent. The Act intends that if a subsequent amendment adversely affects the terms and conditions of service of an existing employee, the written consent of the employee is required to implement such a provision.

Similarly, Section 35 of the Act provides for voluntary retirement in certain circumstances. Section 39B has implemented a contribution-based pension system for employees who join the service after 2075 BS. Sections 55A and 61 of the Act prescribe the basis and procedure for warning, removing or dismissing an employee. There is already a provision for legal action for situations such as incompetence, indiscipline, failure to fulfill responsibilities, corruption or criminal offenses that show moral turpitude.

Therefore, it is not that there is no legal way to take action if an employee does not work or fulfills his responsibilities. The question is its effective implementation. A government that cannot make employees work according to existing laws cannot seek to remove employees en masse on the basis of age or length of service as a suitable means of reform.

Article 304 of the Constitution provides that the laws in force at the time of the commencement of the Constitution shall continue to apply to the extent that they are not inconsistent with the Constitution. The legal provisions protecting the conditions of service cannot be ignored in the absence of an official finding that the provisions of the Civil Service Act are inconsistent with the Constitution. Parliament should seriously examine whether the proposed provision is in accordance with the spirit of the Constitution and the Act.

Politics and administration cannot be completely separate from each other. Both need to collaborate in the formulation and implementation of government policies. However, it is not a democratic system of governance to believe that the professional character and stability of the administration should also change with the change in political leadership.

Winning an election is a mandate to run a government, not a mandate to arbitrarily impose on permanent state institutions. An elected government sets policies and priorities; the civil service implements them in accordance with the constitution, law, and professional standards. It is not uncooperative for employees to advise the political leadership on legal and administrative boundaries.

In Nepal, however, political interference in administration has been a problem for a long time. There are complaints that political access and party affiliation are effective in transfers, promotions, postings, and appointments. Even the trade unions of employees have in some cases become a means of party interests rather than professional interests. This has weakened the neutrality and professionalism of the civil service.

The proposal to remove the trade union provision in the Federal Civil Service Bill and create a grievance redress mechanism can be seen as a positive reform. But if the influence of any political group or youth organization close to the government is established in its place, the bureaucracy will move from one type of political control to another. Making employees independent and professional is a reform, not just changing the means of control.

The past governments and political parties are responsible for the long delay in the Federal Civil Service Bill. The lack of sufficient public information about the provisions added in between and their justification as the bill was drafted, from the relevant ministries to the Ministries of Law and Finance, has also raised questions.

When making laws that have long-term implications on issues such as employee service conditions, retirement, promotion, and adjustment, there should be adequate consultation with the relevant parties. However, if decisions are made without open discussion with employees, administrators, legal experts, and civil society on important aspects of the bill, it weakens ownership and acceptability of the law.

The earlier rush by high-ranking administrative officials to the political leadership to remove the cooling period provision in the bill had also exposed the problem of vested interests and political access within the administration. The employee leadership itself, which is demanding reforms in the civil service, should not prioritize personal interests over institutional interests.

The history of America's 'plunder system' provides an important lesson - the practice of changing administrative personnel along with the change of government ultimately weakens the capacity and credibility of the state. Therefore, a system of selecting personnel based on merit and competition has been established.

Supporters of the 'Schedule F' concept, which President Trump's administration has proposed to weaken the job security of high-level employees, have described it as a way to strengthen elected leadership accountability and administrative control.

Critics have pointed out the risk that it will expose the neutral civil service to political influence and make it easier to replace employees who come from the merit system based on political affiliation.

Nepal should not imitate only one aspect of American practice. Our constitutional structure, administrative history, and state needs are different. A system where the winning party can run the administration as its own political organization cannot be accepted in the name of democratic accountability.

The civil service is not always competent, impartial, and free from corruption. Even within the bureaucracy, there are problems of laziness, irresponsibility, corruption, political nepotism, and a decline in professional values. The entire institution has faced criticism due to the shortcomings of a few employees. However, the solution is not to lump all employees together and punish them collectively.

The government has the right to reform administration, review staffing, eliminate unnecessary positions, make performance appraisals effective, control corruption, and streamline service delivery. But these tasks must be done within the limits of the constitution and the law. Employees who perform poorly should be dealt with through legal processes; capable and experienced employees should not be removed based on the dissatisfaction of the political leadership.

Meanwhile, the civil service has played a continuous role in the running of the state, facing challenges from the political changes of 2017, 2046, and 2063 to the referendum of 2036, earthquakes, floods, and landslides, and the COVID-19 pandemic. Despite changes in political leadership and government, the civil service has functioned as a permanent mechanism to implement state policies and decisions.

It is necessary to give opportunities to the new generation. But generational transition does not only mean displacing experienced employees. Measures can be adopted to open up promotion paths, conduct performance-based evaluations, develop leadership, and manage human resources as needed. The criteria should be based not only on the age or length of service of the employee, but also on his or her ability, performance, and responsibility.

The current bill can be improved by sending it to the Parliament's State Affairs and Good Governance Committee for detailed discussion with the participation of constitutional experts, administrative experts, legal experts, employee representatives, and other stakeholders. While preserving the positive provisions of the bill, provisions that weaken the constitution, the rule of law, and the merit system should be amended.

Nepal needs a capable, accountable, and result-oriented administration. But the attempt to create a bureaucracy loyal to the political leadership in the name of administrative reform further weakens the state. Winning an election is the right to form a government, not the unlimited right to reorganize the administration according to party interests.

The civil service is not a private mechanism of the government; it is a permanent institution of the state. Policies and priorities may change when the government changes, but the professionalism, neutrality, and stability of the administration that runs the state in accordance with the constitution and law must be safeguarded.

There may be some positive aspects to the reform of the Federal Civil Service Bill. However, if it allows for a one-time large-scale removal of serving employees by imposing a 30-year service period or an age limit of 55, thereby expanding political influence, that would not be a reform, but an attack on the merit system.

Nepal must now build a modern public administration based on competence, impartiality, accountability, and professionalism, not a new version of the 'loot system' in bureaucracy.
